title: Blue Hour and Inventory
premise: After her mother's funeral, Lena Yarrow returns to the family house to inventory its contents for sale, discovering her mother's decades of silence encoded in unlabeled boxes and a demolition notice on the neighboring community hall. There she meets Tomas Adeyemi, the last fluent speaker of Yorùbá-inflected pidgin his mother brought from Lagos, who asks Lena to become his final student before the building—and his memory—comes down. As lessons deepen, Lena realizes her mother was Tomas's first student, abandoned mid-sentence, and that the untranslatable sentence he keeps repeating is the apology her mother never delivered. In the hall's final week, Lena completes the translation, speaks it aloud at the demolition as witness rather than owner, and chooses to keep the house—not as inheritance, but as a place where language can continue.
about_author: Petra Oyelaran is a Nigerian-British writer and former archivist whose work explores inheritance, diaspora, and the things families leave unsaid. She lives between London and Ibadan, where she collects recorded voices of elders for a digital language archive.

chapters.title: The Tenant's Key
chapters.summary: Lena, in third-person limited POV, moves into her late mother's house after the funeral, sleeping in the guest room like a renter. She begins a cold inventory of belongings, cataloging objects without memories attached. The emotional beat is numb displacement—grief deferred into paperwork, belonging postponed.

chapters.title: Boxes Without Labels
chapters.summary: Still Lena's POV: she finds sealed boxes marked only with years, containing cassette tapes, a child's exercise book in an unfamiliar script, and a photograph of her mother laughing with strangers. Her brother urges her to hire a skip. The beat is the first crack of curiosity piercing dutiful numbness.

chapters.title: The Man Who Outlived His Language
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Tomas, ninety-one, living above the condemned community hall, rehearsing words no one will answer. He watches movers carry furniture from Lena's house and recognizes the exercise book through a window. The beat is loneliness sharpened into resolve—he decides to knock on a door.

chapters.title: One Final Student
chapters.summary: Tomas arrives at Lena's door asking for an hour a day until the demolition date, six weeks away. Skeptical but unable to refuse him, she agrees. First lesson: sounds her mouth refuses to make. The beat is awkward, comic tenderness—two people negotiating grief through phonetics.

chapters.title: What the Tapes Say
chapters.summary: Lena's POV: she plays a cassette and hears her mother's young voice stumbling through the same lesson, Tomas younger, patient, correcting gently. She realizes her mother studied with him for years, then stopped mid-sentence around the time of some unspoken rupture. The beat is betrayal surfacing inside mourning.

chapters.title: The Sentence He Keeps
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV: he reveals the sentence he has repeated for forty years—one his student left unfinished, which he cannot translate because it requires both speaker and listener to be complete. He asks Lena not to translate it yet, only to hold it. The beat is the weight of custodianship passing to her.

chapters.title: Demolition Notices
chapters.summary: Lena's POV: the council confirms the date; her brother pushes to sell the house fast; Tomas is hospitalized briefly after a fall. Lena, now dreaming in his language, fights on two fronts—for time, for the house. The beat is rising stakes and her first act of ownership instead of tenancy.

chapters.title: Her Mother's Half
chapters.summary: In the last labeled box, Lena finds her mother's unfinished translation attempt and a letter never sent, revealing why she stopped: shame over a broken promise to return to Lagos, and fear that speaking would make leaving real. The beat is devastating clarity—the silence had grammar all along.

chapters.title: Blue Hour
chapters.summary: Climax, alternating POVs: dawn of demolition day, the blue hour. Lena stands before the excavators, translates the sentence aloud—completing it with her mother's half and Tomas's—making both speaker and listener whole. Tomas answers in kind. The beat is catharsis: the untranslatable becomes spoken, witnessed, survivable.

chapters.title: Inventory, Revised
chapters.summary: Resolution, Lena's POV: weeks later, she withdraws the house from sale, relabels every box by hand, and opens the hall's salvaged blackboard in her kitchen for neighborhood children learning Tomas's words. The inventory ends not with ownership but stewardship. The beat is quiet belonging—Lena finally home in a language not hers, kept alive.
